questions.question_text:
Let G be a simple undirected graph. Let TD be a depth first search tree of G. Let TB be a
breadth first search tree of G. Consider the following statements.
(I) No edge of G is a cross edge with respect to TD. (A cross edge in G is between two
nodes neither of which is an ancestor of the other in TD.)
(II) For every edge (u,v) of G, if u is at depth i and v is at depth j in TB, then |𝑖−𝑗| = 1.
Which of the statements above must necessarily be true?
questions.subtopic: Graph traversals, minimum spanning trees, shortest paths
questions.explaination: In a DFS tree of an undirected graph, every non-tree edge is a back edge connecting an ancestor and a descendant, so forward and cross edges do not exist; thus statement I is necessarily true. In a BFS tree, cross edges can connect vertices at the same level ($|i - j| = 0$), so statement II is false.

questions.question_text:
Suppose we are given n keys, m hash table slots, and two simple uniform hash
functions
1h and
2h . Further suppose our hashing scheme uses
1h for the odd keys
and
2h for the even keys. What is the expected number of keys in a slot?
questions.subtopic: Searching, sorting, hashing
questions.explaination: Let $n_1$ be the number of odd keys and $n_2$ be the number of even keys ($n_1 + n_2 = n$). Under simple uniform hashing, each key independently hashes to any slot with probability $1/m$. By linearity of expectation, the expected number of keys in any slot is $\frac{n_1}{m} + \frac{n_2}{m} = \frac{n}{m}$.

questions.subtopic: Graph traversals, minimum spanning trees, shortest paths
questions.explaination: The diagonal entry $(A^3)_{ii}$ counts the number of closed walks of length 3 starting and ending at vertex $i$, so $\text{tr}(A^3) = \sum (A^3)_{ii}$ counts all closed walks of length 3 in $G$. questions.subtopic: Graph traversals, minimum spanning trees, shortest paths
questions.explaination: The two edges with the smallest weights can never form a cycle, so both belong to the MST (A is TRUE). CS

An algorithm has to store several keys generated by an adversary in a hash
table. The adversary is malicious who tries to maximize the number of collisions.
Let k be the number of keys, m be the number of slots in the hash table, and k > m.
Which one of the following is the best hashing strategy to counteract the adversary?

options.A: Division method, i.e., use the hash function h(k) = k mod m.
options.B:
Multiplication method, i.e., use the hash function h(k) = ⌊m(kA −⌊kA⌋)⌋, where
A is a carefully chosen constant.
options.D:
If k is a prime number, use Division method. Otherwise, use Multiplication method.
CS

questions.subtopic: Searching, sorting, hashing
questions.explaination: In universal hashing, the hash function is chosen uniformly at random from a carefully designed universal collection of hash functions independently of the keys. Because the adversary cannot predict which function will be selected at runtime, any fixed choice of malicious keys cannot guarantee worst-case collision behavior.

questions.question_text:
Consider functions Function 1 and Function 2 expressed in pseudocode as
follows:
Function 1
while n > 1 do
for i = 1 to n do
x = x + 1;
end for
n = ⌊n/2⌋;
end while
Function 2
for i = 1 to 100 ∗n do
x = x + 1;
end for
Let f1(n) and f2(n) denote the number of times the statement “x = x + 1” is
executed in Function 1 and Function 2, respectively.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.subtopic: Asymptotic worst case time and space complexity
questions.explaination: In Function 1, the inner loop executes $n + \lfloor n/2 \rfloor + \lfloor n/4 \rfloor + \dots \approx 2n$ times, which gives $f_1(n) = \Theta(n)$. In Function 2, the loop runs $100n$ times, which gives $f_2(n) = \Theta(n)$. Because both functions have exact linear asymptotic growth, $f_1(n) \in \Theta(f_2(n))$ (A is TRUE) and $f_1(n) \in \mathcal{O}(n)$ (D is TRUE).

Let U = {1, 2, 3}. Let 2U denote the powerset of U. Consider an undirected graph
G whose vertex set is 2U. For any A, B ∈2U, (A, B) is an edge in G if and only
if (i) A̸ = B, and (ii) either A ⊊B or B ⊊A. For any vertex A in G, the set of
all possible orderings in which the vertices of G can be visited in a Breadth First
Search (BFS) starting from A is denoted by B(A).
If ∅denotes the empty set, then the cardinality of B(∅) is
.

questions.subtopic: Graph traversals, minimum spanning trees, shortest paths
questions.explaination: The vertex set has $2^3 = 8$ vertices. An edge connects $A$ and $B$ iff $A \subsetneq B$ or $B \subsetneq A$. For the empty set $\emptyset$, every non-empty subset $S \subseteq U$ satisfies $\emptyset \subsetneq S$, meaning all 7 non-empty subsets are direct neighbors of $\emptyset$ at BFS depth 1. A BFS starting at $\emptyset$ must visit $\emptyset$ first, and can then visit the 7 distance-1 neighbors in any of the $7! = 5040$ possible orderings.

questions.question_text:
Let 𝐺 be a directed graph and 𝑇 a depth first search (DFS) spanning tree in 𝐺 that
is rooted at a vertex 𝑣. Suppose 𝑇 is also a breadth first search (BFS) tree in 𝐺,
rooted at 𝑣. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for every such graph 𝐺
and tree 𝑇 ?

options.A: There are no back-edges in 𝐺 with respect to the tree 𝑇
options.B: There are no cross-edges in 𝐺 with respect to the tree 𝑇
options.C: There are no forward-edges in 𝐺 with respect to the tree 𝑇
options.D: The only edges in 𝐺 are the edges in 𝑇

questions.subtopic: Graph traversals, minimum spanning trees, shortest paths
questions.explaination: In a BFS tree $T$, any edge $(u, w)$ in $G$ must connect vertices whose BFS levels differ by at most 1 (i.e., $\text{level}(w) \le \text{level}(u) + 1$). A forward-edge in a DFS tree goes from ancestor $u$ to descendant $w$ with $\text{level}(w) \ge \text{level}(u) + 2$. If such an edge existed in $G$, BFS would explore $w$ directly from $u$ at depth $\text{level}(u) + 1$, contradicting the structure of $T$. Hence, no forward-edges can exist in $G$ with respect to $T$ (C is TRUE).

questions.explaination: The function implements standard Bubble Sort. When sorting an array of $n = 30$ elements in strictly reverse order, every comparison triggers a swap operation. The total number of swaps is $\sum_{i=0}^{n-2} (n - 1 - i) = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} = \frac{30 \times 29}{2} = 435$.

questions.question_text:
Let 𝐺(𝑉, 𝐸) be an undirected and unweighted graph with 100 vertices. Let 𝑑(𝑢, 𝑣)
denote the number of edges in a shortest path between vertices 𝑢 and 𝑣 in 𝑉. Let the
maximum value of 𝑑(𝑢, 𝑣), 𝑢, 𝑣∈𝑉 such that 𝑢≠𝑣, be 30. Let 𝑇 be any breadth-
first-search tree of 𝐺. Which ONE of the given options is CORRECT for every such
graph 𝐺?

options.A: The height of 𝑇 is exactly 15.
options.B: The height of 𝑇 is exactly 30.
options.C: The height of 𝑇 is at least 15.
options.D:
The height of 𝑇 is at least 30.

Organising Institute: IIT Roorkee

questions.subtopic: Graph traversals, minimum spanning trees, shortest paths
questions.explaination: The diameter of $G$ is $\text{diam}(G) = \max_{u,v} d(u, v) = 30$. For any BFS root $r$, the triangle inequality ensures that for the pair $(u, v)$ realizing the diameter, $30 = d(u, v) \le d(r, u) + d(r, v) \le 2 \times \text{height}(T)$. Hence, $\text{height}(T) \ge \lceil 30/2 \rceil = 15$.

Let the maximum value of $d(u, v), u, v \in V$ such that $u \neq v$, be 30. Let $T$ be any breadth-first-search tree of $G$. Which ONE of the given options is CORRECT for every such graph $G$?

options_latex.C: The height of $T$ is at least 15.
options_latex.D: The height of $T$ is at least 30.

The maximum value of 𝑥 such that the edge between the nodes B and C is included
in every minimum spanning tree of the given graph is _________ . (answer in
integer)
questions.subtopic: Graph traversals, minimum spanning trees, shortest paths
questions.explaination: By the cycle property of minimum spanning trees, an edge $e = (B, C)$ is included in every MST if and only if it is strictly lighter than the heaviest edge on every cycle containing $(B, C)$. Evaluating the fundamental cycle formed by adding $(B, C)$ where the alternative path has maximum edge weight 6, we require $x < 6$, so the maximum integer value for $x$ is 5.

questions.question_text:
In a double hashing scheme, ℎ1(𝑘) = 𝑘 mod 11 and ℎ2(𝑘) = 1 + (𝑘 mod 7) are
the auxiliary hash functions. The size 𝑚 of the hash table is 11. The hash function
for the i-th probe in the open address table is [ℎ1(𝑘) + 𝑖 ℎ2(𝑘)] mod 𝑚. The
following keys are inserted in the given order: 63, 50, 25, 79, 67, 24.
The slot at which key 24 gets stored is ___________. (Answer in integer)
questions.subtopic: Searching, sorting, hashing
questions.explaination: Hash values: key 63 at $63 \bmod 11 = 8$; key 50 at $50 \bmod 11 = 6$; key 25 at $25 \bmod 11 = 3$; key 79 at $79 \bmod 11 = 2$; key 67 has $h_1(67) = 1$, stores at 1. For key 24: $h_1(24) = 24 \bmod 11 = 2$ (collision with 79), $h_2(24) = 1 + (24 \bmod 7) = 1 + 3 = 4$. Probe $i=1$: $(2 + 4) \bmod 11 = 6$ (collision with 50). Probe $i=2$: $(2 + 8) \bmod 11 = 10$ (empty). Hence, key 24 is stored in slot 10.
questions.question_text_latex:
In a double hashing scheme, $h_1(k) = k \bmod 11$ and $h_2(k) = 1 + (k \bmod 7)$ are the auxiliary hash functions. The size $m$ of the hash table is 11. The hash function for the $i$-th probe in the open address table is $[h_1(k) + i \cdot h_2(k)] \bmod m$. The following keys are inserted in the given order: 63, 50, 25, 79, 67, 24.
The slot at which key 24 gets stored is \_\_\_\_\_\_\. (Answer in integer)

questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements regarding Breadth First Search (BFS) and
Depth First Search (DFS) on an undirected simple graph G is/are TRUE?

options.A: A DFS tree of 𝐺 is a Shortest Path tree of 𝐺.
options.B: Every non-tree edge of G with respect to a DFS tree is a forward/back edge.
options.C:
If (𝑢, 𝑣) is a non-tree edge of G with respect to a BFS tree, then the distances from
the source vertex 𝑠 to 𝑢 and 𝑣 in the BFS tree are within ±1 of each other.
options.D:
Both BFS and DFS can be used to find the connected components of G.

Organising Institute: IIT Roorkee

questions.subtopic: Graph traversals: BFS and DFS
questions.explaination: In an undirected graph, non-tree DFS edges can only be back edges (B is true). In a BFS tree, cross edges can only exist between the same or adjacent levels, so distances differ by at most $\pm 1$ (C is true). Both can compute connected components (D is true).
questions.question_text_latex: Which of the following statements regarding Breadth First Search (BFS) and Depth First Search (DFS) on an undirected simple graph $G$ is/are TRUE?

options_latex.A: A DFS tree of $G$ is a Shortest Path tree of $G$.
options_latex.B: Every non-tree edge of $G$ with respect to a DFS tree is a forward/back edge.
options_latex.C: If $(u, v)$ is a non-tree edge of $G$ with respect to a BFS tree, then the distances from the source vertex $s$ to $u$ and $v$ in the BFS tree are within $\pm 1$ of each other.
options_latex.D: Both BFS and DFS can be used to find the connected components of $G$.

questions.question_text:
Let 𝐺 be an edge-weighted undirected graph with positive edge weights. Suppose a
positive constant 𝛼 is added to the weight of every edge.
Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE about the minimum spanning
trees (MSTs) and shortest paths (SPs) in 𝐺 before and after the edge weight update?

options.A: Every MST remains an MST, and every SP remains an SP.
options.B: MSTs need not remain MSTs, and every SP remains an SP.
options.C: Every MST remains an MST, and SPs need not remain SPs.
options.D:
MSTs need not remain MSTs, and SPs need not remain SPs.

Organising Institute: IIT Roorkee

questions.subtopic: Graph algorithms: minimum spanning trees and shortest paths
questions.explaination: Adding a constant $\alpha$ to all edge weights preserves the relative order of all spanning trees because every spanning tree has exactly $V - 1$ edges (so all tree costs increase by $(V-1)\alpha$). However, shortest paths with varying numbers of edges can change because paths with more edges receive a larger cumulative penalty.
questions.question_text_latex: Let $G$ be an edge-weighted undirected graph with positive edge weights. Suppose a positive constant $\alpha$ is added to the weight of every edge in $G$. Which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?

options_latex.A: Every MST remains an MST, and every SP remains an SP.
options_latex.B: MSTs need not remain MSTs, and every SP remains an SP.
options_latex.C: Every MST remains an MST, and SPs need not remain SPs.
options_latex.D: MSTs need not remain MSTs, and SPs need not remain SPs.

questions.question_text:
An array 𝐴 of length 𝑛 with distinct elements is said to be bitonic if there is an index
1 ≤𝑖≤𝑛 such that 𝐴[1. . 𝑖] is sorted in the non-decreasing order and 𝐴[𝑖+ 1 . . 𝑛]
is sorted in the non-increasing order.
Which ONE of the following represents the best possible asymptotic bound for the
worst-case number of comparisons by an algorithm that searches for an element in
a bitonic array 𝐴?
questions.subtopic: Searching and divide-and-conquer: bitonic array search
questions.explaination: In a bitonic array, the maximum element can be found in $\Theta(\log n)$ time using binary search on mid-elements. Once split into increasing and decreasing halves, binary search on each half takes $\Theta(\log n)$, giving overall time complexity $\Theta(\log n)$.
questions.question_text_latex: An array $A$ of length $n$ with distinct elements is said to be bitonic if there is an index $1 \le i \le n$ such that $A[1..i]$ is strictly increasing and $A[i..n]$ is strictly decreasing. What is the optimal time complexity to search for a key in a bitonic array?
